scope.source: Westminster Leningrad Codex pointed text (via Sefaria) recorded in the existing book archive

notes: Compared all 85 existing readings with the pointed Westminster Leningrad Codex text supplied in the book archive. Ruth 1:1–22, 2:1–23, 3:1–18, and 4:1–22 have the same source and reader numbering. Kept every verse boundary, Hebrew form, name form, and reference. Revised syntax and cadence where the original English was harder to follow aloud.

Ruth 1:1 preserves the repeated judges/judged wordplay and the foreign-resident sense of לָגוּר. 1:6 retains the visitation and bread, and 1:8 keeps the jussive Qere יַעַשׂ. At 1:13 the comparative sense of מִכֶּם remains provisional. 1:17 expresses the contextual force of the oath as ‘Death alone will separate me from you’. The exclusivity is inferred from the pledge and has no separately written Hebrew word. 1:20–21 preserve Shaddai and the bitter/full/empty contrast.

Ruth 2:1 keeps the Qere מוֹדַע, the kinship setting, and Boaz’s standing. 2:3 expresses the repeated chance root idiomatically. 2:7 retains the difficult sitting-in-the-house clause without emendation. 2:13 keeps the heart image and renders both forms of שִׁפְחָה consistently as slave woman/women, without supplying an age. 2:20 leaves the referent of the kindness unresolved. The distinct young men and young women in 2:21–22 remain.

Ruth 3:3–4 retain the displayed Qere garments and second-person ‘go down’ and ‘lie down’. Ruth 3:5 and 3:17 retain the bracketed Qere ‘to me’. Ruth 3:9 keeps ‘wing’ to echo 2:12 and leaves the garment sense in the notes. Ruth 3:14 retains the read forms for ‘his feet’ and ‘before’. Ruth 3:15 retains the masculine ‘he went into the city’ and an unspecified six measures, followed by the feminine arrival at 3:16.

Ruth 4:3 renders מָכְרָה in the context of a sale being offered, with the acquisition completed at 4:9. Ruth 4:4 translates the ‘uncover your ear’ idiom as telling, preserves the Masoretic shift from ‘you’ to ‘he’ in the conditional, and retains Qere וְאֵדְעָה. Ruth 4:5 retains ‘from Ruth’ (וּמֵאֵת רוּת) and follows the second-person Qere קָנִיתָה, with the first-person Ketiv קניתי recorded here. ‘It’ is supplied for the implied object. The relationship of the land and marriage obligations in this difficult verse remains open for specialist review.

Ruth 4:6 retains the displayed read form לִגְאָל־ and distinguishes an inheritance from a right of redemption. Ruth 4:7–8 preserve redemption, exchange, witnesses and the sandal transfer without equating this with a different legal procedure. Ruth 4:10 maintains ‘acquire’ and the name/inheritance link. Ruth 4:16 takes אֹמֶנֶת as caring for the child. Ruth 4:20–21 retain the distinct forms Salmah and Salmon. Independent specialist, full apparatus and human read-aloud reviews remain pending.
Preserved the repeated going down and hurling in chapter 1, the three references to Tarshish in 1:3, and the exact distinction between the sailors’ gods and YHWH.
At 2:6, “up to my throat” uses the bodily sense of nephesh, where drowning threatens life. At 2:9, the possessive wording of the steadfast love remains open to more than one referent.
At 3:3, retained “great before God” without resolving whether this is an idiomatic superlative. Kept forty days and the three repeated turns in the king’s speech.

Kept the repeated appointed fish, plant, worm, and wind, and “had pity” across 4:10–11. Qiqayon names the uncertain plant at first mention. The inherited scorching wind remains a provisional gloss for the uncommon Hebrew term in 4:8.

notes: Kept the sequence of violence, judgment, and twisted justice in 1:2–4, and the nets and the fishing images in 1:14–17. The collective Chaldean nation takes natural plural agreement. In 1:9, “forward” is one possible sense of qadimah.
Kept the Masoretic “we shall not die” at 1:12 and the possessive “his faithfulness” at 2:4. Retained “wine” at 2:5, following the displayed Masoretic wording.

Preserved the five woes and the repeated bloodshed and violence refrain. The sense of “fury” in 2:15, the unusual term for disgrace or vomit in 2:16, and the referent of “them” at 2:17 remain open to specialist review.

Preserved Selah and the lines about bow, shafts and oath at 3:9, where the Hebrew syntax remains difficult. At 3:13 the anointed is read as the parallel object of salvation. At 3:14 retained the sense of the displayed reading tradition “warriors.” At 3:16 the speaker waits for distress to come upon the raiders.
